## Course description

ME EN 372 covers the analysis foundations of machine design: determining the loads a machine component carries, the stresses and deflections those loads produce, and whether the component will fail by yielding, fracture, fatigue, or buckling. Topics include free-body diagrams and shear and moment diagrams; axial, torsional, bending, and transverse-shear stresses; stress transformation and Mohr's circle; combined loading; deflection and stiffness; static failure theories for ductile and brittle materials; fatigue analysis; pressure vessels, press fits, and curved beams; bolted joints; column buckling; and finite element analysis (FEA) with an emphasis on validating simulation results against hand calculations. Lectures are paired with physical demonstrations, real-world failure case studies, a weekly FEA lab track in Ansys, and a semester-long product-teardown design project.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Free-body and shear/moment diagrams.** Draw free-body diagrams of machine components, determine applied loads, calculate reaction forces and moments, and draw shear and moment diagrams.
2. **Static and fatigue combined loadings.** Calculate stresses in and the life of machine components due to combined static and fatigue loads.
3. **Deflection of structural members.** Estimate the deflection of structural members under combined loading.
4. **Static failure theories.** Select appropriate static failure theories and apply them to predict failure loads and safety factors for various materials and loading conditions.
5. **Stress analysis of components.** Analyze the stresses in pressure vessels, press fits, bolts, and bolted joints.
6. **Buckling prediction.** Calculate buckling predictions for statically loaded compression members.
7. **Finite element analysis.** Use commercial FEA software to create models of simple structures and machine components, and demonstrate decision making using FEA results for engineering applications.
8. **Structured problem solving.** Gain experience using the BYU ME structured problem-solving technique to solve real-world machine design engineering problems, and develop skills to explore solutions to these problems.
9. **Real-world applications and technical communication.** Demonstrate independent learning by applying machine design and analysis concepts to real-world problems, and document the analysis by creating abstracts, introductions, discussions, and figures.

## Textbook and materials

- **Textbook, required:** [*Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design*](https://byu.vitalsource.com/reader/books/9781260407679), 2024 Release, Budynas and Nisbett (McGraw Hill), ISBN 9781260407679. The VitalSource ebook rental is included on Canvas and is charged automatically to your student account. Open **VitalSource** in the Canvas course navigation to access the book. Reading assignments, homework problem numbers, and every section citation in the course materials are based on this edition.
- **How the book is cited.** Course materials cite a section number, as in "Shigley §4-11", and most citations also link straight to that section in the online reader.
- **Calculator:** a non-CAS scientific calculator. This is also the exam calculator (see Exams below).
- **Software:** Ansys and SolidWorks, available in the lab computer room. No personal license purchase is required.
- **Reference sheets:** each exam allows one student-prepared single-sided 8.5 by 11 inch reference sheet plus the BYU ME formula sheet.
- **GitHub account:** free, created in the first week. Coursework is submitted through Canvas; GitHub is where your project files and analysis notes live, and where you can ask an AI assistant for help according to the policy below.

## How the course runs

This course is **flipped**: you review the week's material on your own before class, and class time goes to worked examples, demonstrations, and questions.

- **Before each week (pre-class check-in, 5 points).** Watch that week's slide decks, then answer a short check-in on Canvas. Ten auto-graded questions plus one open box asking what stood out and what you want covered in class. **Due at noon on the day of the week's first lecture.** There are 15 of them, **the two lowest scores are dropped.**
- **Lectures (Mon, Wed, Fri).** Worked examples and short physical demonstrations, "spot it in the wild" everyday examples, and engineering-failure case studies (United 232, the de Havilland Comet, the Hyatt Regency walkway, Challenger, the Quebec Bridge).
- **Labs (Thu).** A progressive FEA track in Ansys: trusses, plates with holes, mesh convergence, beams, combined loading, shafts with keyways, pressure vessels and press fits, bolted joints with pretension and contact, and buckling, each validated against hand calculations. Four sessions are given to the design project instead. Lab writeups are due **the following Wednesday at 5:00 pm** and are worth 10 points.
- **Homework.** Thirteen problem sets, roughly one per week, 100 points each. Each one has two deadlines: an initial submission on **Friday at 5:00 pm Mountain Time** and a corrections submission the following **Wednesday at 5:00 pm**. See "Homework: two deadlines" below. Week 13 (Thanksgiving) has no problem set.
- **Hands-on activities.** Most class demonstrations have a written walkthrough on the [course activity site](https://byu-machine-design.netlify.app/), so you can rebuild or re-measure anything you saw in class. Browse it in week 1 as part of the first check-in.
- **Design project.** A semester-long team product-teardown project (see below).
- **Participation (in-class question, 1 point per meeting).** Class ends with a word written on the board. Open the day's class question on Canvas before you leave, type the word, and add any comments or questions in the essay boxes below. It opens at 12:00 pm and closes at 1:15 pm the same day. There are 40 of them and **the five lowest scores are dropped.**

## Homework: two deadlines

Every problem set is graded in two passes.

| Step | When | What you submit |
|---|---|---|
| Initial submission | Friday, 5:00 pm | A PDF of your worked solutions on Canvas |
| Solution guide posts | Monday, 8:00 am | Nothing to submit. Read it against your own work. |
| Self-grade and corrections | Wednesday, 5:00 pm | Your score for your own initial work, plus corrected solutions to whatever you got wrong |

**Your recorded homework grade is the average of the initial score and the corrected score.** Reading the posted solutions and reworking what you missed is a graded step of the assignment.

If you miss the initial deadline entirely, submit the whole problem set at the corrections deadline instead. The initial score is then a zero, and because the recorded grade is the average of the two, a fully correct late submission records 50%.

## Late work

Every graded item takes a **20% penalty for each day it is late**. After 4 days late the deduction stops there: the work is still accepted for **30% partial credit.** Turning work in late is always worth more than not turning it in.

If illness, university travel, or a family emergency will keep you from a deadline, contact the instructor.

## Design project: product teardown

Teams of 4 or 5, formed within your lab section, buy an inexpensive secondhand product, take it apart, document the machine elements and load paths inside it, and carry one load-bearing component through a full analysis: hand calculations, an FEA model, and a reconciliation of the two. The project closes with a two-part showcase (live lightning talks and a pre-recorded team video) and an individual oral defense.

**Buying the product.** The department card covers up to **\$15 before tax.** [Deseret Industries in Provo](https://deseretindustries.org/) is the default place to shop, and other options work equally well: another thrift store, a cheap new hand tool from Harbor Freight, a free listing on KSL Classifieds, or something already broken at home.

**Where to take it apart.** The [Project Support Center](https://psc.byu.edu/), Engineering Building Room 107, has the tools and bench space. Posted hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 am to 5:00 pm, with two exceptions: it closes Tuesdays from 11:00 am to 1:00 pm for devotional, and closes at 4:00 pm on Thursdays. Book a slot before you go.

| Deliverable | Due (5:00 pm MT) | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Fri Sep 18 | Product-selection criteria sheet and selection memo |
| P2 | Fri Oct 9 | Teardown documentation package (element inventory, photos, teardown video, load-path free-body diagrams, safety record) |
| P3 | Fri Nov 13 | Component analysis plan, hand calculations, and a preliminary FEA model |
| P4a | Wed Dec 9 | Pre-recorded showcase video (3 to 5 minutes) |
| P4 | Fri Dec 11 | Final analysis package: FEA against hand calculations, AI Use Statement, contribution statements |

Your FEA work starts in **week 10**: Lab 9 (Thu Oct 29) is where you idealize the component and get the scope signed off, and Lab 10 (Thu Nov 5) is a supported FEA studio. P3 asks you to hand that model in a week later, running and roughly right. P4 is a refinement and a comparison.

**Oral defense.** Each student defends the team's analysis individually in a short scheduled appointment. It is worth 10% of your course grade, it is closed-AI, and it is graded on your own understanding of the work rather than on the team's result. Sign-up slots are posted on Canvas once the schedule is set, and the sign-up is announced at least two weeks before the first appointment.

**Safety.** Consumer products store energy in ways that are not obvious until it releases. Before the first screw comes out: unplug corded products, remove and store battery packs away from the bench, never open a battery pack, treat capacitors as charged, find preloaded springs before you free them, and wear eye protection. After teardown the product stays powered off permanently. It is never powered again, it is not reassembled into a working tool, and it is not re-donated or given away. Recycle it through the department e-waste stream at the end of the semester. The full procedure is in the project brief on Canvas.

A separate week 1 assignment, **A0**, sets up your GitHub account and repository.

## AI-use policy

This course uses a **layered AI policy**:

- **Exams 1, 2, and 3 are closed-AI, closed-internet, and proctored.** Bringing or using any AI tool during these exams is an Honor Code violation.
- **The design project is open-AI under an "Adopt" posture.** You may use AI tools for engineering analysis, plotting, and drafting, but you must (1) independently validate every calculation the AI produces, and (2) include an **AI Use Statement** appendix in your final report documenting each substantive AI interaction: tool, prompt, output used, and what you validated or changed.
- **The oral defense is closed-AI.**
- It is never a violation to disclose AI use. It is always a violation to use AI on an open-AI task without disclosing it. AI output is not a citable source: if AI surfaces a reference, read and cite the original source.

The section above is the complete policy. Where a specific assignment adds to it, the rule is stated in that assignment's instructions on Canvas. The full policy, with the AI Use Statement format, is on the [AI Use Policy](https://byu.instructure.com/courses/36965/pages/ai-use-policy) page.

## Semester overview

| Weeks | Unit (Shigley chapters) |
|---|---|
| 1-2 | Course intro; stress review (axial, torsion, Mohr's circle); shear and moment diagrams; AI in engineering discussion (Ch. 3) |
| 3-4 | Bending and transverse shear; stress concentrations; combined loading, including 3D stress states (Ch. 3) |
| 5-6 | Deflection: integration, superposition, statically indeterminate members (Ch. 4); **Exam 1**; von Mises stress |
| 7-8 | Static failure theories, ductile and brittle (Ch. 5); fatigue: S-N curves, endurance limit, notch sensitivity, Marin factors (Ch. 6) |
| 9-10 | Fluctuating stresses and the Goodman diagram; combined-loading fatigue; shaft design examples; Miner's rule; reliability (Ch. 6, 7, 20); **Exam 2** |
| 11-12 | Pressure vessels (thin- and thick-walled); press and shrink fits; curved beams; bolted joints, bolt fatigue, and bolt patterns (Ch. 3, 8) |
| 13 | Project showcase, part 1 (Thanksgiving week, Monday only) |
| 14-15 | Buckling: Euler and Johnson columns, eccentric loading, buckling design (Ch. 4); FEA credibility capstone; course review; showcase part 2 |
| Finals | **Exam 3** in the university finals window |

A detailed lecture-by-lecture schedule with homework due dates is maintained on Canvas.

## University policies

Academic honesty means, most fundamentally, that any work you present as your own must in fact be your own work and not that of another, including uncredited AI-generated work (see the AI-use policy above). Violations are handled per university policy ([honorcode.byu.edu](https://honorcode.byu.edu)).
